questions.question: Mention the early methods of food preservation. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Mention the early methods of food preservation.
  • Early civilizations relied on natural preservation methods before mechanical refrigeration existed:
  • • Sun Drying/Dehydration: Removing moisture content from meats, fruits, and grains to
  • prevent microbial growth.
  • • Salting and Curing: Drawing moisture out of food (especially meat and fish) via osmosis.
  • • Fermentation: Using beneficial microbes (like lactobacillus) to produce acids/alcohol that
  • naturally preserve foods.
  • • Smoking: Exposing food to wood smoke, which contains compounds that act as natural
  • preservatives and antimicrobial agents.
  • • Root Cellaring / Ice Harvesting: Storing food in cool underground spaces or using winter ice
  • stored in straw.

questions.question: Mention the types of refrigerated containers used in transport. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Mention the types of refrigerated containers used in transport.
  • Refrigerated containers (reefers) are classified based on their temperature capabilities and design:
  • • Standard Reefers: Closed-type containers with an integrated, electric-powered
  • cooling/heating unit.
  • • Controlled Atmosphere (CA) Reefers: Containers that regulate temperature and actively
  • adjust oxygen () and carbon dioxide () levels to slow down the ripening of fresh produce.
  • • Cryogenic/CO2 Temp-Controlled Reefers: Containers that use dry ice or liquid nitrogen for
  • cooling instead of mechanical compressors, often used for extreme-cold medical shipping.
  • • Ventilated Reefers: Designed for products like garlic or onions that do not need refrigeration
  • but require continuous, fresh air circulation.

questions.question: Mention the limitations of ABC Analysis. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Mention the limitations of ABC Analysis.
  • ABC Analysis (Always Better Control) categorizes inventory into Class A (high value), B (medium
  • value), and C (low value) based on annual consumption value. Its limitations include:
  • • Ignores Criticality: A cheap "Class C" item (like a specialized bolt) may be critical; if it runs
  • out, the entire production line stops.
  • • Based on Past Data: It relies on historical consumption values, which may not accurately
  • predict future spikes or changes in demand.
  • • Monetary Bias: It evaluates inventory solely on cost/value, overlooking factors like lead time,
  • supplier reliability, or shelf life.
  • • Requires Constant Updating: Reclassifications are necessary as market prices and demand
  • fluctuate, which requires ongoing administrative effort.

questions.question: State the importance of shipment conformance in cold chain management. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• State the importance of shipment conformance in cold chain management.
  • Shipment conformance refers to ensuring that the goods arrive exactly in the agreed-upon state—
  • including temperature, packaging integrity, and time windows.
  • • Product Safety: For biological drugs or food items, conformance prevents microbial growth
  • or chemical degradation.
  • • Regulatory Compliance: Meets strict safety standards (e.g., FDA, HACCP) to prevent cargo
  • rejection at borders or checkpoints.
  • • Loss Prevention: Prevents cargo damage claims, insurance disputes, and financial losses due
  • to spoiled inventory.

questions.question: State the importance of infrastructure in cold chain management. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• State the importance of infrastructure in cold chain management.
  • Infrastructure forms the physical backbone of the cold chain.
  • • Ensures Continuity: Adequate infrastructure—including modern cold storage warehouses,
  • pre-cooling facilities, reefer trucks, and power backups (generators)—prevents "breaks" in
  • the cold chain.
  • • Extends Product Shelf Life: Specialized infrastructure preserves food and medicine quality
  • from farms/factories to the end consumer.
  • • Reduces Post-Harvest Losses: High-quality local cold storage reduces food spoilage in
  • agricultural supply chains.

questions.question: Mention the function of refrigerated transportation in cold chain. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Mention the function of refrigerated transportation in cold chain.
  • Refrigerated transportation is the dynamic link that moves products through the cold chain:
  • • Temperature Maintenance: Keeps products within their critical temperature range during
  • transit (whether chilled or frozen).
  • • Air Circulation: Distributes cool air evenly throughout the cargo to eliminate hot spots.
  • • Extended Reach: Enables global and regional distribution of fresh produce and
  • pharmaceuticals to distant markets.

questions.question: State the importance of HML Analysis in inventory control. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• State the importance of HML Analysis in inventory control.
  • HML (High, Medium, Low) analysis classifies inventory based on the unit price of the items:
  • • Customized Purchasing: Helps procurement departments apply strict buying controls over
  • high-unit-price (H) items, while delegating low-unit-price (L) buying to lower staff tiers.
  • • Security & Storage Control: High-price items receive maximum physical security and strict
  • inventory counts.
  • • Cash Flow Optimization: Prevents over-purchasing expensive units, keeping working capital
  • fluid.

questions.question: Explain the role of QR code and RFID coding in cold chain management. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the role of QR code and RFID coding in cold chain management.
  • Automatic identification technologies are crucial for tracking perishable shipments:
  • • QR Codes: Quick Response codes store extensive product data (such as batch numbers and
  • expiration dates) that can be instantly scanned using handheld devices or smartphones to
  • verify product authenticity at various checkpoints.
  • • RFID (Radio Frequency Identification): Active RFID tags can be embedded with temperature
  • sensors. They transmit real-time temperature and location data wirelessly through container
  • walls without requiring line-of-sight scanning, allowing logistics managers to identify thermal
  • anomalies before cargo spoils.

questions.question: Mention the role of pre-cooling in cold chain system. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Mention the role of pre-cooling in cold chain system.
  • Pre-cooling is the rapid removal of field heat from freshly harvested crops immediately after harvest,
  • prior to transport or storage:
  • • Slows Respiration: Dramatically decreases the metabolic and respiration rate of fresh
  • produce, delaying the ripening and aging process.
  • • Limits Moisture Loss: Prevents shriveling and weight loss by reducing transpiration.
  • • Reduces Load on Reefers: Reefers are designed to maintain temperature, not pull it down;
  • pre-cooling ensures the cargo enters the transport vehicle already at the target temperature.

questions.question: State the importance of proper layout in slaughter house operations. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• State the importance of proper layout in slaughterhouse operations.
  • A highly structured layout is mandatory in slaughterhouse operations due to biological hazards:
  • • Prevents Cross-Contamination: A clean linear layout separates "dirty" zones (stunning,
  • bleeding, de-hairing) from "clean" zones (evisceration, chilling, packaging).
  • • Optimizes Workflow: Minimizes handling times, allowing carcasses to move swiftly into
  • refrigerated units to prevent bacterial growth.
  • • Ensures Humane and Safe Workspaces: Provides safe channels for animal movement and
  • ergonomic setups for workers handling sharp tools.

questions.question: Define GOLF Analysis in Material Management. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Define GOLF Analysis in Material Management.
  • GOLF Analysis is an inventory classification method based on the source of supply and procurement
  • channels:
  • • G (Government): Items sourced from government undertakings, public sectors, or canalized
  • agencies, which involve long lead times and rigid payment terms.
  • • O (Ordinary): Sourced from standard open-market suppliers with moderate lead times and
  • negotiable terms.
  • • L (Local): Procured from local suppliers, offering immediate delivery and low transportation
  • costs, requiring minimal safety stock.
  • • F (Foreign): Sourced from international suppliers, characterized by long lead times, customs
  • clearance, currency fluctuations, and high shipping costs.

• State the role of Purchasing Management in material control.

  • terms.
  • • Inventory Optimization: Works with warehouse teams to schedule deliveries (like Just-In-

  • • Supplier Relationship Management: Cultivates a reliable supplier network to guarantee a
  • steady, uninterrupted flow of high-quality raw materials.

questions.question: Discuss how the coding system should be easily understandable and memorable by employees. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss how the coding system should be easily understandable and memorable by employees.
  • An effective material coding system must be designed for human usability, not just database
  • efficiency. To make it easily understandable and memorable for employees, several key principles
  • must be applied:
  • • Logical Hierarchy (Mnemonic/Structured Coding): The code should follow a logical
  • progression (e.g., Category -> Sub-category -> Specific Item). For example, a code like ELEC-
  • CBL-05 immediately tells an employee they are dealing with an Electrical product, specifically
  • a Cable, with a size or variant of 05.
  • • Use of Familiar Symbols & Mnemonics: Avoid long, random strings of numbers (like
  • 948105739). Instead, use letter abbreviations that sound like or represent the item (e.g., RM
  • for Raw Materials, FP for Finished Products).
  • • Consistency and Simplicity: Keep code lengths uniform (e.g., always 6 or 8 characters).
  • Mixing erratic lengths confuses warehouse staff and increases data entry errors.
  • • Avoiding Ambiguous Characters: Do not mix characters that look similar to the eye. For
  • example, avoid placing the number zero (0) next to the letter O, or the number one (1) next
  • to the letters I or L (1I0O).
  • • Visual Aids and Training: Standardized charts, color-coding corresponding to code blocks,
  • and simple training manuals help employees memorize basic codification structures,
  • reducing search times and picking errors on the warehouse floor.

questions.question: Explain the managerial applications of FSN Analysis in material control. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the managerial applications of FSN Analysis in material control.
  • FSN Analysis classifies inventory based on issue frequency and movement speed into Fast-moving
  • (F), Slow-moving (S), and Non-moving (N) items. Managers apply this analysis to make critical
  • operational decisions:
  • • Warehouse Layout and Space Optimization: Fast-moving (F) items are placed near loading
  • docks, dispatch areas, or lower, easy-to-reach shelves to minimize travel time for picking
  • staff. Slow-moving (S) and non-moving (N) items are relegated to back shelves or upper
  • racks.
  • • Obsolescence Management: FSN analysis helps managers identify Non-moving (N) stock that
  • has been sitting idle for long periods. Managers can then decide to write off, sell back, or
  • liquidate this dead stock to free up valuable warehouse space.
  • • Procurement Strategy: Purchasing departments use FSN data to adjust order policies. Fast-
  • moving items are ordered frequently in optimized batches (using EOQ), while slow-moving
  • items are purchased only upon direct request or in minimal quantities.
  • • Inventory Auditing & Cycle Counting: Managers allocate audit resources efficiently. Fast-
  • moving items, which are prone to inventory discrepancies due to frequent handling, are
  • cycle-counted more frequently compared to non-moving items.

questions.question: Describe the role of retail outlets and point-of-sale storage in the cold chain. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the role of retail outlets and point-of-sale storage in the cold chain.
  • Retail outlets and point-of-sale (POS) storage act as the "last mile" and final custody points of the
  • cold chain before products reach the consumer.
  • • Maintaining the Cold Chain Link: Once refrigerated trucks deliver goods to a retail store, the
  • products must be transferred immediately to POS refrigeration units (such as display
  • freezers, open chillers, or back-room cold storage rooms) to prevent thermal bridging and
  • product degradation.
  • • First-In, First-Out (FIFO) Enforcement: POS storage layouts are organized to support
  • FIFO/FEFO (First-Expired, First-Out) inventory rotation, ensuring older stock is placed at the
  • front of the shelf for consumers to buy first.
  • • Visual Quality and Customer Trust: Well-regulated display units preserve the appearance,
  • texture, and nutritional value of fresh meats, dairy, and produce, ensuring consumer safety
  • and satisfaction.
  • • Temperature Monitoring & Alerts: Modern POS display cases are equipped with alarms and
  • digital sensors that alert store staff if a freezer door is left open or if the temperature rises
  • above safe thresholds, preventing large-scale food spoilage.

questions.question: Describe the significance of weight distribution in reefer container stacking. / [CO4] [5x4 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the significance of weight distribution in reefer container stacking.
  • Proper weight distribution is critical when loading and stacking cargo inside a refrigerated (reefer)
  • container. Its significance includes:
  • • Enabling Proper Airflow: Reefers cool their cargo by blowing cold air up through a T-bar
  • floor. If weight is distributed unevenly, or if cargo is stacked too tightly in one area, it blocks
  • the flow of air. This creates "hot spots" where heat builds up, leading to localized spoilage of
  • perishable goods.
  • • Preventing Structural Overload: Reefers are built with insulated walls and specialized floor
  • systems. Concentrating heavy weight in a small area can crack the floor or warp the interior
  • walls, ruining the container's thermal efficiency.
  • • Ensuring Vehicle and Vessel Stability: When reefers are loaded onto trailer chassis, trains, or
  • container ships, an uneven center of gravity can cause safety hazards during transport.
  • During sharp turns or heavy seas, a poorly balanced container can tip over, resulting in
  • catastrophic losses.
  • • Reducing Shifting and Physical Damage: Distributing the weight evenly and using proper
  • dunnage ensures that boxes do not slide, crush, or fall over during transit, preserving both
  • the packaging and the delicate items inside
